title: Old poems
translation: Japanese poetry really is a delight, after all. Put the work of some poor woodcutter into a poem and suddenly it's lovely. Even a wild boar, which is terrifying, turns gentle once you call its lair "the boar's bed".
Poems these days sometimes have one clever line that works. But none of them are like the old poems, where somehow, beyond the words, you feel a whole mood.

Even the old poems that get called bad are better than anything written today. Take Tsurayuki's line "it isn't a thing you twist into thread". People say it's one of the weakest poems in the Kokinshū, but nobody writing now could come up with anything like it. Half the poems from his time sound like that, so I don't see why this one gets picked on. The Tale of Genji even quotes it.

Same with a poem in the Shin Kokinshū that ends "even the pines that are left look lonely on the peak". People call it sloppy, and fine, maybe it is a little loose. But when it was judged at the time, it was rated well, and the retired emperor later said how much it moved him. Ienaga wrote it all down in his diary.

People say poetry is the one art that hasn't changed since the old days. I'm not so sure. Poets today use the same words and the same famous places, but in the old poems they're not the same thing at all. The old ones are easy and direct, with a clean shape and a lot of feeling.
The words of the old popular songs in the Ryōjin Hishō are often moving too. Maybe with people back then, even something they said without thinking sounds wonderful.

literal: Japanese poetry is still a delightful thing.
Even the labour of lowly mountain folk is charming when put into words, and even a fearsome boar becomes gentle when one says 'the boar's resting bed'.
Among the poems of recent times there are some that seem to have one point cleverly put, but there are none that, like the old poems, somehow make one feel a moving atmosphere beyond the words.
Tsurayuki's 'though it is not a thing twisted into thread' is said to be the trash of the Kokinshū, but it does not look like something a person of the present age could compose.
Among the poems of that age, in form and wording, there are many only of this kind.
Why it is this poem alone that has been talked about like this is hard to know.
In the Tale of Genji it is written as 'though it is not a thing'.
In the Shin Kokinshū, the poem that says 'even the remaining pines are lonely on the peak' is talked about, and indeed it may look a little loose in form.
But this poem too, at the time of the joint judgement, was declared good, and afterwards also (the retired emperor) expressed special admiration: so it is written in Ienaga's diary.

Some say the way of poetry alone has not changed from the old days, but well, the same words and poetic places that people compose with now, when the people of old composed them, were not at all the same thing.
Easy and straightforward, the form clean, and the feeling looks deep;
the words of the songs of the Ryōjin Hishō, too, seem to have many moving things.
Is it that, with people of old, even the phrases they spoke carelessly all sound splendid?

notes.quote: 和歌こそなほをかしきものなれ
notes.text: Kenkō was not just a reader of poetry: he was later counted among the four leading poets of the Nijō school, the most important school of his day. So this section is an insider talking about his own art.
'The boar's bed', a set phrase in poetry for the boar's lair. Poetic language makes even a wild boar sound gentle, which is Kenkō's point: words change how things feel.
'Beyond the words': the mood a poem leaves behind after its words have finished. Critics of the time valued this quality very highly.

notes.quote: 糸による物ならなくに
notes.text: Ki no Tsurayuki (c. 872–945) was one of the compilers of the Kokinshū, the first imperial anthology (905). The poem compares the thin, anxious heart at a parting to thread: 'it isn't a thing you twist into thread, and yet at this parting my heart feels thin'. {歌屑|うたくづ}: 'poem trash', a dud. The poem is Kokinshū 415. The Tale of Genji (the Agemaki chapter) quotes it in a slightly changed form.

notes.quote: のこる松さへ峰にさびしき
notes.text: A winter poem in the Shin Kokinshū (1205): the leaves have fallen, and even the pines that are left look lonely on the peak. It is usually attributed to Hafuribe no Narishige; the 1925 edition names Narinaka. People cited it as a bad poem, and Kenkō grants that it may look a little loose.

{衆議判|すぎはん}: judging poems by discussion among several people instead of one judge, here at a poetry contest. Retired Emperor Go-Toba later praised the poem, and Minamoto no Ienaga, the secretary of Go-Toba's Poetry Office, recorded it in his diary.
{歌枕|うたまくら}: the famous places that poets wrote about again and again, often without ever going there.

The Ryōjin Hishō, a collection of popular songs ({今様|いまやう}) put together by Retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa in the twelfth century. {郢曲|えいきよく}: popular song, as opposed to formal poetry. The songs were already old in his day.
